profile.campus: Cincinnati, Hamilton County, Ohio (CyrusOne CIN2 campus)
profile.reading:
Per CyrusOne's own facility page, this 14-story building at 229 West 7th St, Cincinnati, OH 45202 (OSM tags record its earlier name, Broadwing, a Cincinnati-based telecommunications carrier, and alt-name "7th Street Data Center") is CIN2, publishing 143,778 sq ft of technical IT space and 11 MW of IT capacity, described by CyrusOne as the city's primary carrier hotel facility with closed-loop chilled-water cooling, redundant makeup-water feeds, and a FEMA priority-list designation.

This facility is part of CyrusOne's Cincinnati-metro cluster, the company's home market: Wikipedia's CyrusOne entry states Cincinnati Bell purchased a stake in CyrusOne for $525 million in 2010 and divested it in 2015 after CyrusOne's 2013 IPO; the company was originally founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten, and was taken private again in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts (KKR) and Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP) acquired it for approximately $15 billion. The Cincinnati cluster spans buildings in Cincinnati proper, Lebanon, and Butler and Warren Counties in Ohio, plus a related facility across the Ohio River in Florence, Kentucky, reflecting the metro's historical role as CyrusOne's founding market before the company's national and international expansion.

Ohio's Cincinnati metro sits within the PJM Interconnection regional transmission grid, and Duke Energy is the dominant electric utility serving the Cincinnati area; PJM has separately flagged rising data center electricity demand across its multi-state footprint (which spans much of the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest, including Northern Virginia's much larger concentration of facilities) as a factor in its long-term capacity planning. Cincinnati's relatively central US location, moderate climate, and status as CyrusOne's founding home market, rather than proximity to any single hyperscale anchor tenant, are what have kept the company concentrating multiple buildings in this metro even as its larger growth in recent years has shifted toward Texas, Virginia, and international markets.

reading.body:
CyrusOne CIN2 publishes 11 MW of IT capacity in downtown Cincinnati, making it the second-largest disclosed data center in Ohio and roughly 28 percent of the state's published capacity.

The facility occupies 143,778 square feet of IT technical space and uses closed-loop chilled water cooling, a requirement for sustained high-density compute. At typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, 11 MW supports approximately 275 racks. At standard colocation density of 10 kW per rack, it supports roughly 1,100 racks. The published megawatt figure is a hard ceiling on simultaneous load regardless of the facility's stated HPC capability.

Four certifications determine what workloads CIN2 can legally host: PCI DSS for payment-card processing, HIPAA for protected health information, ISO 27001 for certified information-security management, and FISMA for certain federal government work. This compliance posture qualifies the facility for regulated-industry AI inference and data pipelines. Which tenants actually occupy the space is not disclosed.

For Ohio-scale context, only five of 76 mapped data center facilities in the state publish a capacity figure. Those five sum to 38.6 MW. CIN2's share reflects the limits of disclosure as much as infrastructure reality, because most facilities publish no data. For regulated AI workloads requiring Midwest network proximity, 11 MW is sufficient for inference and moderate-scale analytics but constrains large-scale model training.
